---
title: "Probability: Sharing the Total"
---

A deck contains two cards labeled one and one card labeled two. Its potential profile is $(2,1)$.

To answer “What fraction of equally likely cards carry label one?”, we compare the weight two with the total weight three.

Probability expresses that share.

## 🔰 Normalize a nonnegative total {#sec-sample-probability-normalize-a-nonnegative-total}

For discrete possibilities, suppose

$$
P[f]\geq0,
\qquad
0<Z_P=\sum_fP[f]<\infty.
$$

Define

$$
p[f]=\frac{P[f]}{Z_P}.
$$

Then $p[f]\geq0$ and $\sum_fp[f]=1$.

The normalized profile is a probability mass function. It gives $(2/3,1/3)$ for our deck.

The conditions do work: an all-zero profile has no share to distribute; negative weights would produce negative probabilities; an infinite total cannot be normalized by this division.

## 🏵 A probability belongs to an event {#sec-sample-probability-a-probability-belongs-to-an-event}

An event specifies which outcomes count as an answer. For a die, “even” selects $\{2,4,6\}$.

Its probability collects the mass assigned to those possibilities:

$$
\mathbb P(A)=\sum_{f\in A}p[f].
$$

With a fair die,

$$
\mathbb P(\text{even})
=
\frac16+\frac16+\frac16
=
\frac12.
$$

The notation $p[f]$ asks about one value. The notation $\mathbb P(A)$ asks about an event, which can contain several values.

We can now change the question without changing the underlying weights.

## ⚙️ Normalization removes common scale {#sec-sample-probability-normalization-removes-common-scale}

For any constant $c>0$,

$$
\frac{cP[f]}{\sum_g cP[g]}
=
\frac{P[f]}{\sum_gP[g]}.
$$

Thus $(2,1)$ and $(20,10)$ have the same normalized profile.

For two exhaustive alternatives, all probability vectors have the form $(1-\theta,\theta)$ with $0\leq\theta\leq1$. The possible vectors form a line segment. This is the simplest **probability simplex** from the presentation.

More alternatives give more coordinates, still nonnegative and still summing to one. We can return to the geometry later; the essential contract is already visible.

## 🔰 For a continuous model, include the width {#sec-sample-probability-for-a-continuous-model-include-the-width}

Suppose a location $X$ is modeled as uniform along a segment from zero to $0.5$ meters.

Probability is spread along length. A density of $2$ per meter gives

$$
\mathbb P(0.1\leq X\leq0.2)
=
\int_{0.1}^{0.2}2\,dx
=
0.2.
$$

The density's height is two; the event's probability is $0.2$. Height and probability have different units.

Writing the same segment in centimeters changes the density to $0.02$ per centimeter. The corresponding interval from 10 to 20 centimeters still has probability $0.2$.

A density describes **probability per unit of the chosen measure**. Its value can exceed one because its integral supplies the probability.

More generally, an integrable nonnegative profile with positive total can be normalized by

$$
\rho(x)=\frac{P(x)}{\int P(u)\,du}.
$$

The integral specifies the measure being used, here ordinary length.

## 💡 Small intervals and single points {#sec-sample-probability-small-intervals-and-single-points}

Every interval of positive width inside the uniform segment has positive probability. A singleton has zero length and therefore zero probability under this model.

No smallest positive interval has been introduced. A point is a different set from every positive-width interval around it.

A physical reading has finite resolution, so the event described by a displayed number often corresponds to a bin of possible physical values. A continuous model can then answer the finite-resolution question by integrating over that bin.

Some real-valued laws also contain point masses. Saying “the values are real numbers” alone does not establish that every singleton has zero probability.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-probability-try-the-idea}

A variable is uniform on $[0,0.25]$ meters. What is its density, and what is the probability of the interval $[0.10,0.15]$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-probability-work-it-through}

The density is $4$ per meter, since $4(0.25)=1$. The interval has width $0.05$ meters, so its probability is $4(0.05)=0.2$. A density above one has produced an ordinary probability between zero and one.
:::
